title: Electronic Fundamentals
syllabus_overview: Course Coordinator:Adrian McCallum (amccallu@usc.edu.au)School:School of Science, Technology and Engineering
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate discipline-specific knowledge and differentiate between different classes of amplifiers and their characteristics, and apply this knowledge to select amplifiers for specific applications in aircraft systems.
Explain the principles of printed circuit boards (PCBs) used in aircraft electronic systems, including their construction, layout, and fabrication techniques.
Critically analyse the role of semiconductors in electronic systems and justify their application in various aircraft electronic systems.
Assess the performance of Silicon Controlled Rectifiers (SCRs) in aircraft electronic systems and justify solutions to troubleshoot SCR circuits.
Apply the principles of transistor operation to design, analyse, and troubleshoot transistor-based amplifiers used in aircraft electronic systems.
Apply technical knowledge to design basic logic circuits using integrated circuits, considering their function and applications in aircraft electronic systems.

title: Materials and Hardware
syllabus_overview: Course Coordinator:Adrian McCallum (amccallu@usc.edu.au)School:School of Science, Technology and Engineering
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate discipline-specific knowledge and identify various connector types, pins, plugs, sockets, and insulators in accordance with current and voltage rating, coupling, and identification codes.
Demonstrate discipline-specific knowledge in identifying appropriate permanent and non-permanent fasteners for different aircraft applications.
Evaluate the properties and characteristics of materials used in aircraft hardware, applying metallurgical principles and test methods, and justify their use in various applications.
Apply knowledge of transmission systems to analyse and troubleshoot mechanical power transfer in aircraft
Proficiently select and apply appropriate installation and maintenance techniques of pipes and unions with various functions and applications in aircraft systems.
Select, install, and maintain springs and bearings in aircraft components and systems

title: Digital Techniques
syllabus_overview: Course Coordinator:Adrian McCallum (amccallu@usc.edu.au)School:School of Science, Technology and Engineering
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate discipline-specific knowledge of numbering systems and their application in digital systems, enabling effective communication and data representation within aircraft instrumentation.
Explain the basic structure of computers used in aviation, including their components and interactions, to facilitate effective integration of digital systems within aircraft.

Evaluate the role and functionality of microprocessors in aircraft systems and justify optimal solutions for their application in controlling and managing digital processes within aircraft instrumentation.
Assess the operation data buses in digital systems and review their performance in efficient data transfer and communication between various aircraft subsystems.
Apply data conversion techniques to convert analog signals into digital format, ensuring accurate and reliable data acquisition and processing in aircraft systems.
Design and analyse logic circuits used in aircraft instrumentation, ensuring proper functioning and reliability of digital systems within the aircraft environment.

title: Taxation Law and Practice

title: Aircraft Structures & Systems
syllabus_overview: Course Coordinator:Adrian McCallum (amccallu@usc.edu.au)School:School of Science, Technology and Engineering
learning_outcomes: Classify the various structural components of an aircraft, demonstrating an in-depth knowledge of their roles and interactions within the overall system.
Analyse the effects of combined loading on aircraft structures, considering multiple forces and their interactions to ensure structural integrity.
Determine signs of structural failure and identify appropriate methods for joining and repairing aircraft structures to restore their integrity.
Apply structural design principles and tools to optimise aircraft performance, considering factors such as material selection, load distribution, and stress concentration.
Apply technical knowledge on stressed skin construction to design aircraft structures, considering factors such as load distribution and weight optimisation.
Comply with airworthiness requirements for structural strength, ensuring that aircraft structures meet safety regulations and industry standards.

title: Group Project
syllabus_overview: Course Coordinator:Adrian McCallum (amccallu@usc.edu.au)School:School of Science, Technology and Engineering
learning_outcomes: Identify and select the appropriate approach to develop a solution to an aircraft maintenance engineering problem.
Critically appraise the principles and practices of aircraft maintenance engineering required to successfully implement complex solutions.
Apply developed analytical skills to assess and infer aircraft maintenance data.
Apply project management tools and concepts to plan and execute engineering projects to deliver a desired engineering outcome.
Apply the ethics (including professionalism, innovation, sustainability and adaptability) and WHS frameworks, legislation, standards, procedures that guide aircraft maintenance engineering practice
Communicate (both written and oral) with other team members and more broadly within the engineering community.

Demonstrate and apply knowledgeabout endangered animals and their conservation.
Communicate effectively and professionally.

Research, organise, scientifically communicate and present information about animal physiology in a creative and informative way.

title: Marine Vertebrates: Sharks, Seabirds, Fish, Turtles and Whales
syllabus_overview: Course Coordinator:Alexis Levengood (alevengo@usc.edu.au)School:School of Science, Technology and Engineering

Demonstrate and apply knowledge about the evolution, diversity and ecology of marine vertebrates and key issues for their conservation and management.
Critically analyse and evaluate the local and global threats to marine fish, reptiles, birds and mammals, and field data to investigate basic ecology of marine vertebrates.

title: Animal Ecology Field Course
syllabus_overview: Course Coordinator:Bonnie Holmes (bholmes@usc.edu.au)School:School of Science, Technology and Engineering
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate and apply knowledge about; a) the fundamentals of animal ecology as a scientific discipline; b) the questions it asks; c) the evolutionary processes that shape it; and d) the techniques used to study it.
Communicate effectively and professionally.

Systematise and analyse; a) core concepts in animal ecology science; b) the adaptations of animals to their environment, c) biological and ecological levels of organisation, and d) processes that shape the structure of animal communities.

title: Understanding Your World: Introduction to HASS Theory

Recognise and analyse the structure and concepts of academic arguments and theories, and explain these ideas in a clear, concise manner.
Apply basic skills for humanities research and writing, and communicate research ideas and outcomes in a clear, academically-appropriate manner.

syllabus_overview: Course Coordinator:Gregory Watson (gwatson1@usc.edu.au)School:School of Science, Technology and Engineering
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate and apply knowledge of how elements of a still image combine to convey specific information relevant to the study of animal ecology, and the basics of how a digital camera works.
Critically analyse and solve problems in photography to illustrate animal identification, habitats, behaviour and physiology in a scientific manner.
Construct and capture images to convey specific scientific information for research and communication in animal ecology.

title: Statistics with Teeth: Understanding Ecological Data
syllabus_overview: Course Coordinator:David Schoeman (dschoema@usc.edu.au)School:School of Science, Technology and Engineering

Employ logical reasoning and empirical support to arrive at independent conclusions.
Communicate effectively and coherently in written and oral forms, using correct terminology, appropriate formats.

Develop the ability to locate, analyse and synthesise relevant scholarly sources across a range of analog and digital settings and/or mediums.

title: Propeller Systems
syllabus_overview: Course Coordinator:Adrian McCallum (amccallu@usc.edu.au)School:School of Science, Technology and Engineering

Assess the quality and performance of aircraft propellers based on blade element theory and fundamental principles.

Construct computational models to synchronise propeller systems and ensure smooth operation.
Apply blade element theory and technical skills to design aircraft propellers, ensuring optimal performance and meeting user requirements.

Communicate in a variety of media to demonstrate critical dialogue, originality and engagement in the discipline

Critically analyse and solve problems in physiology by collecting, accurately recording, interpreting, drawing conclusions from and presenting data, according to scientific conventions.
Research, organise, scientifically communicate and present information about comparative physiology in a creative and informative way.

title: Medical Genetics
syllabus_overview: Course Coordinator:Anna Kuballa (akuballa@usc.edu.au)School:School of Health - Biomedicine
learning_outcomes: Describe and explain the concepts and principles behind the genetic regulation of health and disease and how our understanding of these processes can lead to improved health outcomes for individuals and communities.
Collect, accurately record, interpret and draw conclusions from scientific data.
Describe and critically analyse ethical issues associated with genetic research, counselling and diagnostics.
Gather, synthesise and critically evaluate information from a range of sources.

title: Blood Banking and Transfusion Sciences
syllabus_overview: Course Coordinator:Yoke Lin Fung (ylfung@usc.edu.au)School:School of Health - Biomedicine
learning_outcomes: Explain, describe, analyse and interpret antigen antibody interactions as they relate to blood banking and transfusion sciences and transplantation disorders
Investigate and analyse clinical issues in blood banking and transfusion sciences and their link to the local and global community
Demonstrate an understanding of the professional and ethical responsibilities inherent in blood transfusion and tissue transplantation in clinical practice.

Understand the stages and challenges to providing an adequate blood supply, including blood donors, blood donation, blood collection and processing, the range of blood and blood products and how each is used.

title: Immunology
syllabus_overview: Course Coordinator:Kate Mounsey (kmounsey@usc.edu.au)School:School of Health - Biomedicine

Articulate some aspects of the place and importance of immunological science in the prevention and treatment of disease
Utilise scientific research and link immunological issue to a broader population or social context.

Identify and apply professional responsibilities according to appropriate national decision making frameworks for human research ethics.
Describe the current regulatory and ethical environment for clinical trials with unapproved therapeutic goods and the role of the different stakeholders involved in this process.
Demonstrate proficiency in documentation practices required in the commencement of a clinical trial.
Explain and describe the principles of Good Clinical Practice (GCP) in consent processes, quality data collection and compliance with reporting requirements.

Ethically collect, record, interpret, and communicate findings from experiments using physiology knowledge.

learning_outcomes: Critically analyze the development of alternative transport options considering changing resource availability and other external shocks and stresses (e. g. natural hazards, conflicts) that place different demands on infrastructure.

Investigate and explore innovative techniques to progress towards a world with fossil free transport systems.
Evaluate the sustainability of different transport systems in meeting the needs of civil society.

learning_outcomes: Discuss solutions to address environmental engineering challenges.

Apply knowledge and skills to make high level, independent judgements relating to environmental engineering for a range of ethical or management functions in varied specialised contexts.
Develop, plan, implement and evaluate short, medium and long term plans and schedules for an environmental problem.

learning_outcomes: Use and apply design codes e.g. AS/NZS 1170.0, AS/NZS 1170.1 and AS 3600; determine design loads and load combinations for strength and serviceability and understand their importance in limit state design.
Describe and explain the nature of concrete and steel and how they work as a composite members i.e. reinforced concrete.

Communicate (in your group or to an audience) your design, ie. procedures, outcomes and recommendations, in a manner acceptable to the engineering profession.

learning_outcomes: Investigate and synthesise information and concepts in the selection of landfill liner construction materials and methods to synthesise solutions for various applications.

Critically examine and apply expert judgement when assessing and establishing the design philosophy to be adopted for storm water drainage systems, flood mitigation problems and water resources systems.

Design and analyse major components of stormwater systems, focusing on traditional detention basin design, but with alternative contemporary solutions stemming from integrated water cycle management (such as grass swales and wetlands).

Demonstrate advanced technical knowledge of soil behavior and geological mapping to classify geotechnical properties for functional design and construction.

learning_outcomes: Professionally analyse, design and evaluate social media strategies.
Demonstrate legal, ethical and professional social media practice.
Critically analyse different organisation's objectives and social media strategy performance.
Critically use mainstream social media platforms.
Produce and disseminate high quality digital content for social media platforms
Apply skills in client communication, liaison and social media account management.

title: Social Media Internship
syllabus_overview: Course Coordinator:Karen Sutherland (ksutherl@usc.edu.au)School:School of Business and Creative Industries
learning_outcomes: Develop professional networks and relationships with industry professionals.
Professionally analyse, design and deliver strategies, assessments or products for a client in the relevant sector.
Apply and reflect on the professional standards of practice, code of conduct and workplace culture.
Communicate professionally across all interpersonal and written modes.

title: Professional Creative Writing Practice: Industry Engagement
syllabus_overview: Course Coordinator:Lee McGowan (lmcgowa1@usc.edu.au)School:School of Business and Creative Industries
learning_outcomes: Identify and document industry practices in one or more aspects of the Creative Writing and Publishing Industries
Critically reflect on, analyse and evaluate demonstrated skills in an aspect of creative writing and publishing
Apply the concepts and theories of creative writing and publishing industries, including problem solving, analytical and research skills and evaluation in a professional practice situation.
Responsibility and accountability for own learning and professional practice.

title: Creative Writing and Editing for Publication
syllabus_overview: Course Coordinator:Ross Watkins (rwatkins@usc.edu.au)School:School of Business and Creative Industries
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate industry-specific skills involved in writing and editing for publication, including substantive and copy editing fundamentals
Create and edit manuscripts demonstrating critical understandings of ethics and aesthetics
Demonstrate effective communication skills and work cohesively within a team environment.
Demonstrate planning and problem-solving skills in order to meet publication deadlines
Analyse and reflect upon publishing practices using scholarly conventions, critical thinking and the application of theory to practice

title: Newsroom
syllabus_overview: Course Coordinator:Peter English (penglish@usc.edu.au)School:School of Business and Creative Industries
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate production efficiency.
Produce material for publication that is created ethically and professionally.
Connect with the regional community to generate content for publication.
Produce news of a publishable standard.

title: Counselling for Addiction Disorders
syllabus_overview: Course Coordinator:Trudi Flynn (tflynn@usc.edu.au)School:School of Law and Society
learning_outcomes: Comprehend contemporary theoretical models of substance and behavioural addictions
Reflect on connections between theory and lived experience (case studies) in addiction disorders
Demonstrate assessment and case formulation for addiction disorders
Consider addiction factors in diverse populations
Understand the principles of Harm Minimisation in addiction disorders
Demonstrate academic integrity skills

title: Theories of Counselling: From Freud to Integrative Practice
syllabus_overview: Course Coordinator:Daniel Eaton (deaton@usc.edu.au)School:School of Law and Society
learning_outcomes: Apply your knowledge of theory to a particular case study.
Distinguish between analytic, affective, behavioural and cognitive theories and systems, and demonstrate an understanding of the historical context and theory of human development.
​Engage with the process of self-reflection and know which of your own values supports or hinders the process of counselling.
​Articulate an awareness of the ethical and cultural basis of the studied theories and the implications for counselling diverse populations.
Demonstrate effective communication through written reports, complying with accepted APA 7th ed. guidelines.

title: Cognitive Behaviour Therapy: Skills and Applications
syllabus_overview: Course Coordinator:Catherine Creamer (ccreamer@usc.edu.au)School:School of Law and Society
learning_outcomes: Explain and describe the theoretical background and evidence base to CBT.
Understand the background to mental health disorders and issues that may be ethically treated with CBT for the promotion of health and wellbeing for populations served by counsellors
Compare and contrast techniques and research related to the clinical application of CBT, and critically appraise the indications and contraindications for use of CBT in practice.
Implement client psychoeducation regarding the nature of CBT and ways to minimise symptoms.
Examine the evidence base of CBT in treating different presenting issues, as well as its strengths and limitations in practice.
Demonstrate effective communication through written reports and oral presentations, complying with accepted APA 7th ed. guidelines.

title: Counselling Integrative Practice
syllabus_overview: Course Coordinator:Katrina Andrews (kandrews1@usc.edu.au)School:School of Law and Society
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate their consolidating ability to critically reflect on own identity and practice for life long learning
Demonstrate their consolidating knowledge regarding working with children, youth, and adults with various complaints

Demonstrate their consolidating knowledge and skills applying person-centred counselling skills with CBT, Group, Strength-based Models, to improve mental health and wellbeing in clients, using practice-based evidence principles.
Articulate an emerging integrative counselling identity and counselling practice
Demonstrate a mature ethical mindedness
Demonstrate mature academic integrity skills

title: Group Processes and Practice
syllabus_overview: Course Coordinator:Katrina Andrews (kandrews1@usc.edu.au)School:School of Law and Society
learning_outcomes: Understand and identify basic theoretical frameworks in the group work context.
Introduce, Conduct, and Process a single group activity that aims to generate discussion and to focus the group
Identify and Discuss the interpersonal processes adopted by group members and group leaders according to group work theory
Demonstrate beginning academic writing skills in the reflective essay genre, using APA 7th ed. conventions

title: Therapeutic Communication Skills
syllabus_overview: Course Coordinator:Daniel Eaton (deaton@usc.edu.au)School:School of Law and Society
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate skill and growth in self-reflection and self-awareness.
Identify and critically analyse therapeutic communication skills and ethical practice within a counselling context for the promotion of health and wellbeing.
Demonstrate developing academic writing skills, including the application of APA7 conventions.
Identify ethical practices and standards within various therapeutic environments.
Comprehend and apply academic scholarship.

title: Counselling Children and Youth
syllabus_overview: Course Coordinator:Katrina Andrews (kandrews1@usc.edu.au)School:School of Law and Society
learning_outcomes: Understand the historical trends that inform contemporary counselling practice with children and youth
Demonstrate ability to generalise person centred counselling skills to children and youth populations
Critique current accepted strength-based and positivist models and frameworks when counselling children and youth
Demonstrate ability to integrate evidence-based practice models when working with children and youth with developed person-centred counselling skills, with goal to improve mental health and wellbeing
Critically apply evidence-based frameworks for counselling children and youth to diverse children and youth populations
Apply accepted written academic skills and APA 7th ed. referencing/formatting conventions to written assignments

title: Counselling for Crisis, Trauma and Loss
syllabus_overview: Course Coordinator:Shannon Hodges (jhodges1@usc.edu.au)School:School of Law and Society
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate a sound understanding of the current theories and models that inform trauma work
Compare contemporary models of grief, illustrating a knowledge of the strengths and weaknesses of each
Effectively role play a contemporary evidence based intervention for trauma or grief, incorporating trauma informed principles to address health and wellbeing of populations served by counsellors.
Demonstrate knowledge of how to work with trauma and grief with diverse populations
Understand the ethical considerations when working with people suffering trauma and/or grief
Effectively demonstrate oral and written communication skills, complying with accepted APA 7th ed. conventions.

title: Counselling Placement and Development 1
syllabus_overview: Course Coordinator:Kelly Thomson (kthomson1@usc.edu.au)School:School of Law and Society
learning_outcomes: Identify, articulate and describe beginning skills in developing a critically reflective practice including how your values, beliefs, and ethical mindedness impinge on your practice.

Recognise principles and competencies required in supervision practices. Assess and identify ways of strengthening the supervisee/supervisor relationship and the relationships with colleagues in the agency and on campus.
Begin to analyse organisational systems and processes and identify inequalities.
Apply the values and ethical principles of counselling according to USC Student Code of Conduct, Student Placement Agreement and ACA and PACFA Codes of Ethics, acting in a professional manner.
Demonstrate respect and valuing others with an understanding of and sensitivity towards the issue of cultural diversity, gender and disability.
Demonstrate graduate level academic reflective skills in oral and written format, and compliance with accepted APA 7th ed. conventions.

title: Counselling Older Australians
syllabus_overview: Course Coordinator:Trudi Flynn (tflynn@usc.edu.au)School:School of Law and Society
learning_outcomes: Comprehend contemporary social issues impacting the older Australian
Understand the impact of aging on Australians, physically and mentally
Have an appreciation of the unique ethical considerations when working with older Australians
Apply known issues and problems of aging in Australia, to the Indigenous context
Demonstrate competency in applying evidence based interventions for common issues and complaints of older Australians with the end-goal of improved mental health and wellbeing.
Demonstrate developed academic integrity and research skills for life long learning.

title: Strengths Based Counselling: Collaborative Approaches
syllabus_overview: Course Coordinator:Daniel Eaton (deaton@usc.edu.au)School:School of Law and Society
learning_outcomes: Analyse, apply and evaluate the use of a strength-based approach to counselling from a client and counsellor perspective.
Identify and articulate the history and principles of strength-based collaborative counselling.
Critically reflect on your own values and beliefs in relation to the counselling process using a strengths-based approach.
Demonstrate and apply your understanding of the ethical responsibilities and professional requirements underpinning the use of a strengths-based approach.
Demonstrate and utilise a solution-focused approach to build on progress, change, health and wellbeing for the clients that counsellors serve.
Demonstrate effective communication through written reports and oral presentations, complying with accepted APA 7th ed. guidelines.

title: Counselling Placement and Development 2
syllabus_overview: Course Coordinator:Kelly Thomson (kthomson1@usc.edu.au)School:School of Law and Society
learning_outcomes: Extend on beginning skills in developing a critically reflective practice by reflecting on skills learnt as a result of the 2 x practicums that were outside of the curriculum

Recognise principles and competencies required in supervision practices. Assess and identify ways of building a strong supervisee/supervisor relationship in a second setting, as well as building strong relationships with existing and new colleagues in the second agency as well as on campus.
Describe the professional, ethical and legal issues in practice and of your own ethical behaviour, within the setting of your second agency, including the continuing importance of self care

Continue to apply the values and ethical principles of counselling according to UniSC Student Code of Conduct, Student Placement Agreement and ACA and PACFA Codes of Ethics, always acting in a professional manner.
Demonstrate respect and valuing others with an advanced understanding of and sensitivity towards the issue of cultural diversity, gender and disability.
Demonstrate graduate level academic reflective skills in oral and written format, and compliance with accepted APA 7th ed. conventions

title: Positive Psychology for Counselling
syllabus_overview: Course Coordinator:Trudi Flynn (tflynn@usc.edu.au)School:School of Law and Society
learning_outcomes: Review and apply the research that supports the principles, skills and strategies of positive psychology, and critically assess the claims of positive psychology to promote health and wellbeing.

Identify the changes in lifestyle you want to make and demonstrate through self-reflective writings that you are moving towards living in a positive psychological state with increased stable happiness.
Understand and identify theoretical and practical concepts of Positive Psychology for counselling.
Create and plan Positive Psychology interventions, apply and reflect on effectiveness and outcomes.
Demonstrate effective communication through written reports and oral presentations, complying with accepted APA 7th ed. guidelines

title: Advanced Counselling Skills 1: Interpersonal Processes
syllabus_overview: Course Coordinator:Michele Crosbie (mcrosbie@usc.edu.au)School:School of Law and Society
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate advanced development and capabilities in the skills of engaging with a client.
Demonstrate an advanced understanding of the implications of pluralistic practices of a professional counsellor in practice.
Develop and apply deep knowledge of theoretical techniques and skills that underpin cognitive behaviour approaches and person-centred approaches to counselling.
Articulate and unpack the connection between the knowledge and the processes of counselling and the counselling relationship.
Make sophisticated linkages between the counselling discipline and the sociocultural context and multicultural context in which clients live.
Demonstrate academic scholarship

title: Professional Development 1: Clinical Practice
syllabus_overview: Course Coordinator:Catherine Creamer (ccreamer@usc.edu.au)School:School of Law and Society
learning_outcomes: Acquire a body of knowledge and skills that will extend your understanding of the counselling profession and in particular the recent developments in counselling practice both nationally and internationally/
Apply communication skills to present a clear and coherent and independent exposition of counselling knowledge and skills to groups within the community.
Continue to be committed to on-going personal and professional development enriched by diverse cultural knowledge.
Acquire technical knowledge and professional skills to discern and evaluate your counselling practice with clients and to innovatively develop creative initiatives that match the needs of clients.
Apply the values and ethical principles of Counselling according to the USC Student Code of Conduct, ACA and PACFA Code of Ethics and acting in a professional manner.
Evidence of ability to reflect on experience of practice and provide a descriptive evaluation of professional skills acquired, tested and practiced.

title: Developmental and Family Counselling
syllabus_overview: Course Coordinator:Katrina Andrews (kandrews1@usc.edu.au)School:School of Law and Society
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate a comprehensive understanding of the history, models, and principles of family and relationship counselling, including frameworks for responding to domestic and family violence.

Critically reflect on your own family of origin, relational dynamics, and experiences, and apply this self-awareness to ethically support clients affected by complex family issues, including domestic violence.

Apply theoretical models such as Bowen, structural, and strategic family therapy to simulated case scenarios, integrating trauma-informed and safety-focused approaches relevant to domestic violence contexts
Demonstrate awareness of personal values and belief systems regarding families, relationships, and violence, and evaluate their impact on ethical and culturally responsive counselling practice.

Critically examine the diversity of family structures and experiences—including multicultural, gendered, and intergenerational perspectives—and assess the implications for supporting wellbeing in families affected by violence and relational distress.
Demonstrate scholarly capacity in written submissions through clear expression, integration of current academic literature on family and DV counselling, and adherence to APA style.

title: Expressive Therapies: Counselling with the Creative Arts
syllabus_overview: Course Coordinator:Trudi Flynn (tflynn@usc.edu.au)School:School of Law and Society
learning_outcomes: Critically reflect on and analyse the history, principles and practices of expressive therapies as a counselling intervention.
Apply and evaluate the appropriateness of expressive therapies as a counselling intervention.
Demonstrate and apply expressive therapies concepts and skills with clients in a knowledgeable, responsible and ethical manner.
Reflect critically on your own values and beliefs in relation to using expressive arts in the counselling process.
Demonstrate ability to use expressive therapies with a diverse range of clients.
Critically appraise research studies related to the clinical application of various creative arts modalities.

title: Internship 1
syllabus_overview: Course Coordinator:Kelly Thomson (kthomson1@usc.edu.au)School:School of Law and Society
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate integration of counselling theory, knowledge and skills in a counselling practice.
Demonstrate critical self-reflection of your own practice, including your values, beliefs and your understanding of ethical responsibilities.
Understand the relevance and importance of ongoing supervision and professional development within counselling practice.

Demonstrate relevant skills of assessment and intervention with a particular client group and apply creativity and initiative in in the application of this knowledge to other client groups. Be familiar with the organization, daily functioning, ethical concerns and demands and cultural diversity of a counselling practice.

Articulate understanding and integration of counselling theory and skills in an agency setting, positive, respectful working relationships with clients, colleagues and community members, valuing of others with an understanding of and sensitivity towards cultural diversity, gender and disability, in a group supervision setting.

title: Counselling Children and Young People
syllabus_overview: Course Coordinator:Trudi Flynn (tflynn@usc.edu.au)School:School of Law and Society
learning_outcomes: Identify, analyse and apply the principles and practices of child and adolescent counselling.
Develop a practice framework for counselling children based on an integrative model for children and adolescents.
Develop and demonstrate skills in counselling children and adolescents (forming a therapeutic relationship, and supporting change).
Understand and apply ethical responsibilities and professional requirements underpinning counselling children and adolescents.
Demonstrate academic scholarship

title: Professional Development 2: Grief, Loss and Trauma
syllabus_overview: Course Coordinator:Trudi Flynn (tflynn@usc.edu.au)School:School of Law and Society
learning_outcomes: Acquire a body of knowledge and skills that will extend your understanding of the counselling profession and in particular the recent developments in counselling practice both nationally and internationally.
Have the technical knowledge and skills to discern and evaluate your counselling practice with clients recovering from loss and trauma.
Respond sensitively to clients experiencing existential or spiritual challenges.
Demonstrate an understanding of the in-session application of concepts, theories and interventions of grief counselling and grief therapy

Create and sustain an ethical therapeutic relationship with persons through a bereavement and mourning process and assist them to make meaning of their experience linking individual wellness to community wellbeing.

title: Internship 2
syllabus_overview: Course Coordinator:Kelly Thomson (kthomson1@usc.edu.au)School:School of Law and Society
learning_outcomes: Develop, articulate, assess and evaluate learning goals in a professional practice setting using counselling theory, skills, knowledge and values.

Continue to demonstrate critical and creative self-reflection on your own practice, values and beliefs and evaluation of clinical counselling practice and your understanding of ethical responsibilities
Understand the relevance and importance of ongoing supervision and professional development within counselling practice.

Demonstrate relevant skills of assessment and intervention with a particular client group and apply creativity and initiative in in the application of this knowledge to other client groups. Be familiar with the organization, daily functioning, ethical concerns and demands and cultural diversity of a counselling practice.

Articulate advanced understanding and integration of counselling theory and skills in an agency setting, positive, respectful working relationships with clients, colleagues and community members, valuing of others with an understanding of and sensitivity towards cultural diversity, gender and disability, in a group supervision setting.

title: Counselling and Mental Health
syllabus_overview: Course Coordinator:Catherine Creamer (ccreamer@usc.edu.au)School:School of Law and Society
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate advanced knowledge of the mental health field by critically examining understanding of what constitutes mental illness, health and recovery including evidence-based diagnosis and treatment paradigms.
Analyse and evaluate the role of counselling, pharmacotherapy and other treatment supports used with individuals impacted by mental health issues.
Critically analyse and synthesise the complex knowledge required to enable tailoring and facilitation of individualised mental health counselling interventions.
Apply a client-directed and outcome informed approach in developing a comprehensive treatment plan for a client presenting with mental health issues in an ethical and responsible manner.
Apply specialist mental health counselling knowledge in the development of a tailored group counselling intervention. Evidence of ethical consideration in the intervention design.
Demonstrate a developing scholarly capacity in written submissions, incorporating clarity of written expression, integration of academic literature, and adherence to APA style.

title: Counselling and Addictions
syllabus_overview: Course Coordinator:Trudi Flynn (tflynn@usc.edu.au)School:School of Law and Society
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate mastery of the theoretical concepts underpinning addictions including biomedical, psychological and social frameworks, and the classification of treatments for a variety of addictions.
Analyse and evaluate the role of counselling, pharmacotherapy and other treatment supports used with individual, couples and family impacted by addiction issues.
Apply knowledge and skills learned in a counselling session.
Critically reflect on their own facilitation of Motivational Interviewing within a counselling session.
Apply a client-directed and outcome informed approach in developing a comprehensive treatment plan for a client presenting with addictions in an ethical and responsible manner.
Demonstrate a developing scholarly capacity in written submissions, incorporating clarity of written expression, integration of academic literature, and adherence to APA style.

title: Solution Focused Therapeutic Approaches
syllabus_overview: Course Coordinator:Catherine Creamer (ccreamer@usc.edu.au)School:School of Law and Society
learning_outcomes: Articulate and demonstrate capability in both knowledge and skills of SFBT.
Articulate and demonstrate capability in both knowledge and skills of Motivational Interviewing.
Identify a client's need through the interviewing process and develop strategies for working towards a solution utilising the advanced skills of SFBT.
Develop solutions based on SFBT principles that anticipate and overcome resistance to sustained change for clients in their socio-cultural context.
Draw on research and best practice in SFBT counselling to propose new solutions to client's contemporary problems.
Critically reflect on their own facilitation of Solution Focused Brief Therapy within a counselling session.
Demonstrate a developing scholarly capacity in written submissions, incorporating clarity of written expression, integration of scholarly literature and adherence to APA style.

title: Ethics and Reflective Practice
syllabus_overview: Course Coordinator:Trudi Flynn (tflynn@usc.edu.au)School:School of Law and Society
learning_outcomes: Analyse critically and reflect on the complex theories, principles and practices of ethics in relation to counselling practice.
Critically analyse counselling case scenarios and apply sound ethical decision making to those cases and articulate and defend your ethical decision.
Understand and discuss ethical dilemmas that may arise in counselling and synthesise appropriate responses for diverse contexts and multicultural cases.
Identify personal values and beliefs and biases that may have an impact on your ethical decision in counselling practice.
Evidenced understanding of reflective practice as it pertains to counselling;
Analyse outcomes from reflective practice and deduce implications for practice based on personal learning, and develop an intended course of action;
Demonstrate a developing scholarly capacity in written submissions, incorporating clarity of written expression, integration of academic literature, and adherence to APA style.

title: Research Project A
syllabus_overview: Course Coordinator:Catherine Creamer (ccreamer@usc.edu.au)School:School of Law and Society
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate a mastery of theoretical knowledge and reflect critically on theory and professional practice through a research project.
Develop the cognitive and technical skills to ethically investigate, analyse and synthesise complex counselling information and develop interventions or research for specific needs.
Communicate and justify your findings with clarity through written and oral presentations.
Demonstrate academic scholarship

Reflect critically on your own values, attitudes and beliefs in relation to the use of mindfulness practices for yourself and with your clients.
Synthesise and evaluate the body of research on particular aspects of mindfulness practice and its use in mental health.
Apply a mindfulness based intervention as self-care in your counsellor trainee role.
Create a mindfulness-based intervention for an identified group of clients.
Demonstrate understanding of the ethical responsibilities and professional requirements which underpin mindfulness-based interventions.
Demonstrate a developing scholarly capacity in written submissions, incorporating clarity of written expression, integration of academic literature, and adherence to APA style.

Demonstrate an ability to engage with family systems and sociocultural systems within the context of counselling in an ethical and professional manner.
Demonstrate expertise in the knowledge and skills of therapeutic integration.
Identify and develop decision making pathways in counselling that maintain sustainable outcomes for clients and families.
Articulate and demonstrate your personal approach to counselling and psychotherapy.

Demonstrate presentation skills and the ability to summarise research outcomes
Produce a substantial counselling based research report ready for publication

title: Understanding Crime
syllabus_overview: Course Coordinator:Nadine McKillop (nmckillo@usc.edu.au)School:School of Law and Society

Apply different theories to explain specific crimes and crime patterns.
Critique various crime theories from a scientific viewpoint and assess their potential impact on criminal justice policy and practice.
Develop and support key arguments using evidence-based research and analysis
Demonstrate high-quality written and oral communication skills, including scholarly writing and reference practices.

title: Punishment and Corrections
syllabus_overview: Course Coordinator:Emily Moir (emoir@usc.edu.au)School:School of Law and Society

Identify the specific needs of different correctional clients and groups
Develop and support their own arguments using evidence-based research and critical analysis
Outline and explain the main contemporary processes involved in addressing offending behaviour
Apply scholarly writing, research, and reference practice

title: Introduction to Criminology
syllabus_overview: Course Coordinator:Lara Christensen (lchriste@usc.edu.au)School:School of Law and Society

Explain and describe the key elements and theories of crime and criminal justice.
Analyse the causes of crime and social impacts.

Develop and support their own arguments using evidence-based research and critical analysis
Apply scholarly writing, research, and reference practice

syllabus_overview: Course Coordinator:Timothy Prenzler (tprenzle@usc.edu.au)School:School of Law and Society

Critically evaluate ethical issues and standards, the nature and causes of misconduct, and the rationales for integrity strategies in the criminal courts.
Summarise and critique ethical issues and standards, the nature and causes of misconduct, and the rationales for integrity strategies in corrections.
Apply scholarly writing, research and reference practice.

Explain and critique forensic science practices
Apply scholarly writing, research, and reference practice
Develop and support their own arguments using evidence-based research and critical analysis

title: Youth Justice & Restorative Justice
syllabus_overview: Course Coordinator:Nadine McKillop (nmckillo@usc.edu.au)School:School of Law and Society

Articulate the nature, causes, and consequences of youth crime and victimisation and apply these to specific youth crime problems.
Critically analyse current issues relevant to youth justice.
Describe and evaluate evidence-informed practices for preventing and responding to youth crime and victimisation.
Apply scholarly writing, research, and reference practices

syllabus_overview: Course Coordinator:Susan Rayment-McHugh (srayment@usc.edu.au)School:School of Law and Society
learning_outcomes: Research and synthesise relevant sources relating to careers in criminal justice or related professions.
Actively prepare for transition into employment.
Demonstrate analytical and critical thinking skills.
Demonstrate self-reflection and self-evaluation.
Demonstrate advanced interpersonal and written communication.

syllabus_overview: Course Coordinator:Madeline Lee (mlee3@usc.edu.au)School:School of Law and Society
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate and apply relevant knowledge of the principles of criminal law and procedure.
Apply critical thinking, analysis and reasoning to generate appropriate responses to issues and problems in criminal law.
Communicate effectively in various modes.
Develop and support their own arguments using evidence-based research and critical analysis

title: Applied Crime Prevention
syllabus_overview: Course Coordinator:Timothy Prenzler (tprenzle@usc.edu.au)School:School of Law and Society

Communicate principles of situational crime prevention, CPTED and security management as they relate to real world settings.
Apply principles of situational crime prevention, CPTED and security management in a real environment.
Summarise key themes of effective situationally-focused crime prevention.
Critical thinking and analysis of diverse sources of information

Demonstrate an understanding of the relevant issues and the strategies and resources available to support the safe, responsible and ethical use of ICT in learning and teaching, including parental/carer involvement where appropriate.

title: Diversity and Inclusion

Demonstrate a range of verbal and non-verbal communication strategies to support student engagement.

Apply your knowledge, understanding and skills as a professional educator to interpret, implement, integrate, and adapt learning for individual needs and abilities. title: Teacher as Researcher
