syllabus_overview: Course Coordinator:Shazi Saremi (ssaremi@usc.edu.au)School:School of Science, Technology and Engineering
learning_outcomes: Identify and describe device and network security vulnerabilities.
Identify data points and device/network behaviours that reveal vulnerabilities in the computer network.
Explain the role of data access restrictions, white-listing, administrative privileges, and related controls from a multi-actor perspective in an organisational context.
Diagnose device and network security vulnerabilities using online resources.
Work as part of a team to effectively undertake and communicate security activities.
Demonstrate effective written and oral communication skills to present research and findings to specialist and non-specialist audiences.

title: Cryptography, Blockchain and Information Security
syllabus_overview: Course Coordinator:Georg Lippold (glippold@usc.edu.au)School:School of Science, Technology and Engineering
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate knowledge of cryptography fundamentals for security and authentication.
Compare and contrast data security and privacy of cryptographic protocols outlining their strengths and vulnerabilities.
Demonstrate the qualities of professionalism, leadership and digital collaboration.
Communicate research and findings to specialist and non-specialist audiences.

title: Cyber Intelligence
syllabus_overview: Course Coordinator:Dennis Desmond (ddesmond@usc.edu.au)School:School of Science, Technology and Engineering
learning_outcomes: Plan a strategy to collect OSINT while maintaining operational security
Apply open source collection techniques used by cyber investigators
Develop online tradecraft skills to conceal intent and obfuscate your identity to facilitate online collection of investigatory information.
Recognise and mitigate vulnerabilities In Identity data and Personal Electronic Devices (PEDs).
Perform identify resolution to authenticate and differentiate online identities and analyse findings .
Detect illicit online behaviour
Communicate online investigatory findings and competencies

title: Introduction to Cybersecurity
syllabus_overview: Course Coordinator:Jayamine Alupotha (ralupotha@usc.edu.au)School:School of Science, Technology and Engineering
learning_outcomes: Describe basic network structures and technologies and how they can be exploited in an organisational context
Examine the range of technical and human factors (threats and vulnerabilities) that impact networks and the governance and compliance requirements.
Communicate cyber-security incidents or potential incidents using technical and non-technical language and recommend timely and effective mitigation actions to a broad range of stakeholders.
Evaluate evolving technologies and the potential cybersecurity implications of their deployment and implementation.

title: Complex Cyber Investigations Management
syllabus_overview: Course Coordinator:Clive Harfield (charfiel@usc.edu.au)School:School of Science, Technology and Engineering
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate understanding of professional investigation management and professional practice
Demonstrate in-depth knowledge of the management of securing and presenting evidence relating to cybercrime and digital data integrity breaches.
Critically analyse the role of digital deviancy and its investigation in society including how each might be a source of criminal and/or social harm
Use decision-making and problem-solving
Communicate research and findings to specialist and non-specialist audiences.

title: Ethics in Digital Investigation and Cyber Security
syllabus_overview: Course Coordinator:Declan Humphreys (dhumphreys@usc.edu.au)School:School of Science, Technology and Engineering
learning_outcomes: Explain, apply, and justify ethical frameworks and decision-making in cybersecurity and digital investigations.
Reflect and recognise differing ethical perspectives in cybersecurity and digital investigations.
Identify harms, conflicts, and risks in cybersecurity and digital investigations.
Undertake and communicate research, analysis, and conclusions to specialist and non-specialist audiences.

title: Digital Crime Scene Management
syllabus_overview: Course Coordinator:Graeme Edwards (gedwards@usc.edu.au)School:School of Science, Technology and Engineering
learning_outcomes: Identify the different forms of cybercriminal, their motivations and skillsets.
Analyse and discuss the methodologies used in managing a digital crime scene including preparation of an investigation plan.
Analyse and discuss the many forms of digital evidence available and their relevance to a digital investigation.
Demonstrate the requirements of competently handling digital evidence.
Interrogate digital evidence to identify its value to an investigation
Understand and apply legal options available to the civil investigator

Identify and explain the different legal considerations an investigator must understand when planning and commencing a digital crime scene examination including evidence preservation and capture as well as preserving the chain of custody.
Demonstrate effective collaboration within a team
Communicate the outcomes of your inquiries to non-technical audiences such as senior managers.

title: Cryptography, Blockchain and Security
syllabus_overview: Course Coordinator:Nayson Machin (nmachin@usc.edu.au)School:School of Science, Technology and Engineering
learning_outcomes: Identify and explain the evolution of cryptographic protocols.
Explain the cryptographic function of block ciphers and their value in proving the authenticity of data transactions.
Identify and discuss the elements of the key exchange process.
Apply a range of security applications suitable to secure a network connected device.
Compare and contrast the value to data security and privacy of cryptographic protocols outlining their strengths and vulnerabilities.
Demonstrate the qualities of professionalism, leadership and digital collaboration.
Communicate research and findings to specialist and non-specialist audiences.

title: Introduction to Device & Network Security
syllabus_overview: Course Coordinator:Nayson Machin (nmachin@usc.edu.au)School:School of Science, Technology and Engineering
learning_outcomes: Explain device and network fundamental concepts.
Diagnose data points and device/network behaviours that reveal vulnerabilities in the computer network.
Evaluate the role of data access restrictions, white-listing, administrative privileges, and related controls from a multi-actor perspective in an organisational context.
Communicate research and findings in systematic ways to specialist and non-specialist audiences.

title: Psychology of Cybercrime
syllabus_overview: Course Coordinator:Dennis Desmond (ddesmond@usc.edu.au)School:School of Science, Technology and Engineering
learning_outcomes: Critique key components and processes involved in historical through to contemporary forms of cybercrime offending.
Apply behavioural and criminological frameworks that explain cybercrime offending.
Identify attributes of cybercrime victimisation and the response system.
Use analytical skills to construct cybercrime profiles, prevention and awareness models.
Explain key ethical and practice challenges associated with cybercrime prevention and response from a multi-stakeholder perspective.

title: Cyber Laws and the Rules of Evidence
syllabus_overview: Course Coordinator:Elizabeth Chang (echang@usc.edu.au)School:School of Science, Technology and Engineering
learning_outcomes: Identify and apply criminal statutes and case laws relating to the lawful seizure, storage and examination of evidence located in an online environment.
Identify and apply national and international jurisdiction and data sovereignty laws in planning an online investigation.
Identify and apply privacy laws in a data breach scenario including regulatory compliance with mandatory data breach laws.
Professionally and ethically respond to case developments and justify actions when managing digital investigations as part of an incident response team.
Recognise and apply the principles of evidence law in a criminal and privacy context.
Communicate expert findings to specialist and non-specialist audiences.

title: Digital Forensics 1
syllabus_overview: Course Coordinator:Andrew Lee (alee1@usc.edu.au)School:School of Science, Technology and Engineering
learning_outcomes: Use decision making and problem solving to identify, analyse, and understand digital evidence and digital artefacts
Solve complex technology related crimes.
Seize and secure digital evidence in a safe and admissible manner.
Document and report on interactions with digital evidence; Identify and utilise the appropriate software and hardware tools to support an investigation.
Identify and explain the types of specialised technical and investigative methodologies used in digital forensics.
Prepare and present digital forensic reports in accordance with ethical and evidentiary requirements.

title: Network Forensics
syllabus_overview: Course Coordinator:Andrew Lee (alee1@usc.edu.au)School:School of Science, Technology and Engineering
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate knowledge of network forensics evidence acquisition processes and techniques.
Identify and explain current cyber attacks, relevant network controls, infrastructure interception points, standard and advanced security intelligence platforms
Develop practical skills to detect, extract and analyse all relevant forensic artefacts.
Develop and produce reports suitable for admission as case evidence, that describe identification, search and seizure requirements and examine and analyse provided evidence.

title: Digital Forensics 2: Advanced concepts in Digital Forensics
syllabus_overview: Course Coordinator:Andrew Lee (alee1@usc.edu.au)School:School of Science, Technology and Engineering
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate the differences in various digital technologies and operating systems.
Analyse various encoding schemes, file systems, and applications.
Justify digital forensic methodologies and processes.
Collect and examine digital evidence in a safe and sanitary manner.
Produce detailed digital forensic reports and documentation in accordance with ethical and evidentiary requirements.
Exploit relevant digital artefacts as a team to identify evidential material and solve complex crimes

title: Cyber Industry Placement/Research Project
syllabus_overview: Course Coordinator:Clive Harfield (charfiel@usc.edu.au)School:School of Science, Technology and Engineering
learning_outcomes: Critique key components and processes involved in the understanding and deployment of cyber security controls and countermeasures.

Apply behavioural, ethical, information systems and criminological frameworks that explain workplace cyber security policies, techniques, and practice challenges associated with working within a cyber security environment from a multi-stakeholder perspective
Identify and analyse attributes of cyber security risk assessment, prevention, detection and response system as they relate to the workplace setting.
Use analytical skills to demonstrate value and new knowledge and insights required within the workplace setting.
Critically reflect on your own practice and values.
Act in accordance with prescribed code of conduct/ethics, including communicating respectfully with clients, colleagues and community members.

title: Interactive Narrative: Fundamentals
syllabus_overview: Course Coordinator:Colleen Stieler-Hunt (cstieler@usc.edu.au)School:School of Business and Creative Industries
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate knowledge of a range of basic narrative elements used in interactive narrative writing.
Adapt and apply learning principles to an interactive narrative piece.
Be empowered to develop original ideas and produce creative artefacts in alignment with industry standards.
Demonstrate creativity in evaluating the effectiveness of interactive narrative pieces on agency and emotional engagement

title: Introduction to Game Design
syllabus_overview: Course Coordinator:Scott Roberts (sroberts1@usc.edu.au)School:School of Business and Creative Industries
learning_outcomes: Analyse and describe games in terms of player experience, game design theory, impact, and target audience.
Work as part of a team to iteratively design, develop, and present a game accounting for player experience, game design theory, impact, and target audience.
Document the game design and development process in terms of player experience, game design theory, impact, and target audience.

title: Introduction to Games Programming
syllabus_overview: Course Coordinator:Scott Roberts (sroberts1@usc.edu.au)School:School of Business and Creative Industries
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate foundational knowledge in programming for games
Apply and communicate technical skills, frameworks and organisational practices to contribute to the development of games
Design, research, and develop game components for public distribution

title: Game Art: Introduction to 2D & 3D
syllabus_overview: Course Coordinator:Scott Roberts (sroberts1@usc.edu.au)School:School of Business and Creative Industries
learning_outcomes: Describe and explain the technical, creative and aesthetic decision making processes associated with the design process to a technical audience.
Reflect on how an audience would perceive the assets in a real-time application.
Design a concept brief and project reflections using the method of project quality criteria.
Apply 2D or 3D design skills to create assets useful in game development.

title: Introduction to Game Production
syllabus_overview: Course Coordinator:Nathaniel Leach (nleach@usc.edu.au)School:School of Business and Creative Industries
learning_outcomes: Develop classic digital games accounting for games design context, game structure, and broader impact.
Analyse how elements of games and teams work together to create engaging player experiences.
Extend on an existing classic game design and communicate your game design to a lay audience and a professional audience.

title: Experimental Game Design
syllabus_overview: Course Coordinator:Scott Roberts (sroberts1@usc.edu.au)School:School of Business and Creative Industries
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate knowledge of theories relating to game design and production, game mechanics, and game elements, and how they integrate to form game experiences.
Critically analyse games through given frameworks and design theories.
Design and create prototypes of experimental games based on theories of design and game design principles.

title: Game Art: Characters & Vehicles
syllabus_overview: Course Coordinator:Scott Roberts (sroberts1@usc.edu.au)School:School of Business and Creative Industries
learning_outcomes: Discuss the technical, creative and aesthetic decision making processes associated with the design process.
Develop an understanding of how an audience would perceive the assets in a real-time application.
Acquire advanced optimization skills in a 2D or 3D art, that will avoid wasting resources, or affect the performance of a real-time application.
Discover innovative ways in which design tools may be applied to produce creative solutions to a diverse range of design challenges.

title: Professional Games Programming
syllabus_overview: Course Coordinator:Arden Sedmak (asedmak@usc.edu.au)School:School of Business and Creative Industries
learning_outcomes: Analyse, evaluate, and develop programs in the C# language.
Work in a structured and modular manner, consistent with the needs of a team development environment.
Communicate programming concepts with simplicity and precision when collaborating with non-programmers, both verbally and in the form of a technical specification.
Create code to specification in developing and applying games programming solutions.

title: Interactive Narrative: Puzzles and Quests
syllabus_overview: Course Coordinator:Ginna Brock (gbrock@usc.edu.au)School:School of Business and Creative Industries
learning_outcomes: Critically analyse the relationship between narrative and interactivity
Demonstrate a broad body of knowledge regarding puzzle design in both offline and digital formats.
Demonstrate knowledge in the practices of interactive narrative design and development
Integrate and apply knowledge from specific fields and disciplines; such as narratology, ludology, and psychoanalytical studies.
Creative production of interactive stories that effectively balance narrative aspects and user experience,

title: Video Game Analysis and Design
syllabus_overview: Course Coordinator:Alexander Smith (asmith16@usc.edu.au)School:School of Business and Creative Industries
learning_outcomes: Research and describe the theoretical and analytical frameworks that apply to games.
Assess and describe the social values that games reflect and propagate.
Analyse, critique and design digital games based on theoretical and reflective frameworks.
Organise analysis in clear, concise, and accurate written forms.

title: Game Art: Virtual Environments
syllabus_overview: Course Coordinator:Jake Fitzakerley (jfitzakerley@usc.edu.au)School:School of Business and Creative Industries
learning_outcomes: Describe and explain the technical, creative and aesthetic decision making processes associated with the design process to a technical audience.
Reflect on how an audience would perceive the assets in a real-time application, in terms of ethical issues.
Critically reflect on practice during the design and creation of an immersive virtual environment
Apply 2D or 3D design skills to create assets useful in 3D digital environments.

title: Experimental Games Programming
syllabus_overview: Course Coordinator:Justin Carter (jcarter3@usc.edu.au)School:School of Business and Creative Industries
learning_outcomes: Design, research, and develop game components for distribution.
Apply technical skills and frameworks to contribute to the development of games.
Communicate and implement knowledge of a programming speciality and justify its value and contribution to the game development process.
Reflect, evaluate, and justify your ability to close knowledge, skill and technology gaps in a self-directed manner.

title: Game Studio A
syllabus_overview: Course Coordinator:Justin Carter (jcarter3@usc.edu.au)School:School of Business and Creative Industries
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate initiative and judgement in planning, management and decision making in a simulated professional environment
Use and apply professional ethical principles and practices
Demonstrate cognitive and technical skills to produce an innovative games product
Collaborate in a project team effectively and produce games industry products

title: Advanced Games Programming
syllabus_overview: Course Coordinator:Scott Roberts (sroberts1@usc.edu.au)School:School of Business and Creative Industries

Communicate knowledge about your chosen programming speciality and its value and contribution to the game development process.

title: Interactive Narrative: Characters and Worlds
syllabus_overview: Course Coordinator:Alexander Muscat (amuscat@usc.edu.au)School:School of Business and Creative Industries

Analyse characters, cultures and worlds in a way that enables critical and philosophical thought about sustainability and ethical practices in managing resources and needs.
Be empowered to develop original ideas and produce creative artefacts in alignment with industry standards.

title: Anterior Hip Arthroplasty Supervised Clinical Practicum
syllabus_overview: Course Coordinator:Nicole Masters (nmasters@usc.edu.au)School:School of Health - Anatomy
learning_outcomes: Perform a minimum of 5 DAATHA procedures under supervision, with the student and/or supervisor free to extend the number of supervised cases (up to a maximum of 20) to demonstrate sufficient level of competence, including practice surgical and competencies.

Practice surgical planning and preparation including pre-operative radiological investigations, considering specific patient and technical factors as well as prosthesis selection and management of medical and anaesthetic issues.
Communicate with clinical staff and patients, and collaborate within teams, encompassing the needs and perspectives of others.

Evaluate the patient's post-operative recovery and rehabilitation and manage postoperative pain, including ward management, prevention and management of complications and institution of an appropriate rehabilitation plan.
Practice within ethical, legal and professional boundaries and comply with the Australian Medical Association Code of Ethics and the Australian Orthopaedic Association Code of Conduct.
Critically reflect on your own professional practice in relation to short-term surgery outcomes and provision of patient-centred care.

title: Foundations of Anterior Hip Arthroplasty
syllabus_overview: Course Coordinator:Nicole Masters (nmasters@usc.edu.au)School:School of Health - Anatomy
learning_outcomes: Explain the hip and pelvis in anatomical, physiological and pathological terms.
Demonstrate a comprehensive technical knowledge of hip prostheses, materials and tribology.
Apply appropriate clinical and radiological evaluation techniques to identify candidates for DAATHA.
Demonstrate comprehensive knowledge of the technical aspects required to perform direct anterior approach total hip arthroplasty.
Demonstrate a safe approach to complication management.
Develop appropriate perioperative protocols to improve patient experience and outcomes.

title: Introduction to Sport and Exercise Science
syllabus_overview: Course Coordinator:Ross Clark (Rclark@usc.edu.au)School:School of Health - Sport and Exercise Science
learning_outcomes: Define the fundamental principles in sport and exercise science.
Discuss key topics and issues in sport and exercise science and their impact on health, performance, and professional practice.
Recognise the significance of sport and exercise science sub-disciplines for professional development.
Explain and demonstrate how principles from various sport and exercise science sub-disciplines effectively address challenges in real-world practical settings.
Outline common issues in sport and exercise by applying foundational scientific concepts.

title: Physical Activity and Health
syllabus_overview: Course Coordinator:Florin Oprescu (foprescu@usc.edu.au)School:School of Health - Sport and Exercise Science
learning_outcomes: Describe the role of health and exercise scientists in the broad structure and success of the Australian health system.
Explain the roles of sedentary behaviour and physical activity in the aetiology, prevention, and management of chronic conditions, mental health, and disability.
Explore the roles of public policies, agencies and social determinants of health in promoting PA and reducing sedentary behaviour.

Develop evidence-based health promotion strategies to increase PA and reduce sedentary behaviour in the general population and diverse priority communities, allowing consideration of social determinants of health.
Identify and assess populations at risk of insufficient physical activity.
Identify and use the common processes and equipment required to conduct accurate and safe PA assessments.

title: Introduction to Coaching Science
syllabus_overview: Course Coordinator:Davide Bastia (dbastia@usc.edu.au)School:School of Health - Sport and Exercise Science
learning_outcomes: Define key coaching and exercise training concepts and terminology relevant to professional practice.
Explain coaching requirements for training and developing athletes across various ages and diverse backgrounds, including consideration of social determinants of health.
Define methods for teaching sport skills or tactics to diverse populations based on the needs of individuals.
Know and apply ethical and professional conduct in interactions with athletes, coaches, and officials.
Describe and assess effective communication skills across various coaching scenarios.

title: Surgical Skills Simulation in Anterior Hip Arthroplasty
syllabus_overview: Course Coordinator:Nicole Masters (nmasters@usc.edu.au)School:School of Health - Anatomy
learning_outcomes: Reflect on live surgery in anterior hip arthroplasty.
Demonstrate the cognitive and technical competencies required to conduct the direct anterior approach for total hip arthroplasty (DAATHA).
Communicate and collaborate with the surgical team to achieve optimal patient outcomes.

Practice within ethical, legal and professional boundaries as they pertain in compliance with the Australian Medical Association Code of Ethics and the Australian Orthopaedic Association Code of Conduct.
Evaluate personal orthopaedic surgical competencies in relation to professional development.

title: Game Studio: Polish and Publish
syllabus_overview: Course Coordinator:Arden Sedmak (asedmak@usc.edu.au)School:School of Business and Creative Industries

Clearly and effectively communicate design ideas, solutions and concepts at multiple levels, for example with clients, supervisor and team members.
Apply advanced Problem solving, analytical and research skills to your practical work.
Be responsible and accountable for your own learning and professional practice and in collaboration with others in a game production setting.

title: Biomechanics I
syllabus_overview: Course Coordinator:Max Stuelcken (mstuelck@usc.edu.au)School:School of Health - Sport and Exercise Science
learning_outcomes: Describe human movement using appropriate terms and concepts
Use the laws of motion to explain the cause of human movement
Identify inter-relationships between biomechanical variables
Perform calculations based on biomechanical data
Apply biomechanical principles to human locomotion, activities of daily living, and dynamic sporting skills
Disseminate the findings of biomechanical experiments ethically, clearly and succinctly

title: Exercise Prescription and Programming II
syllabus_overview: Course Coordinator:Dan van den Hoek (dvandenhoek@usc.edu.au)School:School of Health - Sport and Exercise Science
learning_outcomes: Interpret the interactions between physiological, biomechanical, and psychological factors and their influence on exercise performance.
Interpret pre-exercise screening and evaluation tools to determine current health status and associated exercise risk in healthy populations.

Design and implement exercise programs for low-risk individuals that align with their goals and physiological needs, including selecting and applying appropriate technology to support in-person and telepractice service delivery.
Interpret the outcomes of exercise testing procedures and equipment in assessing different aspects of human performance.
Compare and contrast different methods of periodisation used in exercise programming, considering individual needs, training goals and timelines.
Demonstrate safe and effective use of resistance training equipment in accordance with industry standards and individual client needs.

title: Anterior Hip Arthroplasty Appraised Clinical Practicum
syllabus_overview: Course Coordinator:Nicole Masters (nmasters@usc.edu.au)School:School of Health - Anatomy
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate safe practice performing a minimum of 20 direct anterior approach for total hip arthroplasty (DAATHA) procedures unsupervised.
Practice within ethical, legal and professional boundaries and comply with the Australian Medical Association Code of Ethics and the Australian Orthopaedic Association Code of Conduct.
Critically reflect on your own professional practice for continuous improvement purposes.
Audit clinical outcomes including complications and radiological outcomes in DAATHA.
Communicate with clinical staff and patients throughout the DAATHA surgical procedure to assure patient-centred care.
Lead a multidisciplinary team of healthcare professionals to assure appropriate case management and patient-centred care.

title: Anatomy and Physiology for Exercise
syllabus_overview: Course Coordinator:David Jenkins (djenkins@usc.edu.au)School:School of Health and Behavioural Sciences
learning_outcomes: Identify and describe anatomical and physiological functions from scenarios shown on diagrams, images and in text.
Apply spatial visualisation skills to human anatomical and physiological models and identify orientation, placement and relationship to overall structure.

title: Sport and Exercise Psychology
syllabus_overview: Course Coordinator:James Clark (jclark5@usc.edu.au)School:School of Health - Sport and Exercise Science
learning_outcomes: Differentiate and summarise major concepts, theories, and frameworks used in sport and exercise psychology.
Apply psychological theory to sport and exercise settings across diverse populations.
Distinguish between relevant psychological frameworks and their applicability to a sport and exercise context.
Summarise and apply psychological foundations of behaviour change in sport and exercise.
Demonstrate the ability to communicate effectively and respond appropriately to assist clients from diverse populations to change their health and physical activity behaviours.

title: Exercise Prescription and Programming I
syllabus_overview: Course Coordinator:Robert Buhmann (rbuhmann@usc.edu.au)School:School of Health - Sport and Exercise Science
learning_outcomes: Explain exercise prescription and program design decisions using knowledge of human factors influencing participation and performance.

Identify and apply how pre-exercise, risk assessment and movement screening results inform decisions about safe exercise participation and risk management and understand when onward referrals are warranted.
Explain and apply the principles of exercise progression in client-centred program design.

Outline and apply safe and effective programming prescription of exercise to suit the needs and abilities of healthy adults and diverse populations allowing consideration of social and cultural determinants of health.
Recognise and apply ethical and professional conduct in interactions with athletes, coaches, work environments.

title: Functional Anatomy
syllabus_overview: Course Coordinator:Max Stuelcken (mstuelck@usc.edu.au)School:School of Health - Sport and Exercise Science
learning_outcomes: Describe human movement using the appropriate anatomical and biomechanical terms and concepts to allow effective communication with colleagues and fellow practitioners.
Explain how the basic mechanical properties of the structures of the musculoskeletal system relate to their different functional roles during human movement.
Apply anatomical knowledge to explain the roles of, and relationships between, structures of the musculoskeletal system during human movement.
Interpret research relating to the functional anatomy of the musculoskeletal system during human movement and the impact of loading and exercise.
Summarise functional changes in the musculoskeletal system across the lifespan and in response to injury, illness, or impairment.

title: Motor Control and Learning
syllabus_overview: Course Coordinator:David Borg (dborg@usc.edu.au)School:School of Health - Sport and Exercise Science
learning_outcomes: Identify and explain the different theoretical approaches and principles of voluntary movement.
Explain the contribution of the motor and sensory systems during performance, and the factors affecting the initiation and control of action.
Interpret the typical research methodologies and measurements used in motor control and learning.
Communicate information on key topics in motor control and learning in written and oral modes.
Use practice design to optimise learning and performance.
Explain and apply the principles of motor learning and/or motor control in a practical setting.

title: Exercise Physiology I
syllabus_overview: Course Coordinator:Bridgette O'Malley (bomalley@usc.edu.au)School:School of Health - Sport and Exercise Science
learning_outcomes: Explain and differentiate between the function, regulation, and integration of the energy transfer, respiratory, cardiovascular, muscular, neural, and endocrine systems during exercise.
Identify food sources and integrate the role and function of key macronutrients and micronutrients involved in exercise.
Apply literature, information, and learning resources from multiple sources to support decision-making in exercise physiology.
Interpret and discuss exercise physiology research literature using the principles of the scientific method.
Conduct valid, accurate, and reliable tests and measurements of physiological function during exercise including screening and safety procedures and understand when to cease a test.
Analyse and interpret results from laboratory experiments in exercise physiology and understand when onward referral is required.

title: Sports and Exercise Medicine
syllabus_overview: Course Coordinator:Caitlin Hill (chill3@usc.edu.au)School:School of Health - Sport and Exercise Science
learning_outcomes: Understand and describe the ethical and other professional considerations in sports and exercise medicine care.
Demonstrate knowledge and understanding of sports and exercise medicine theory and principles.

Use knowledge of early post-injury intervention techniques to manage an acute sports injury, including first aid principles and delivery of an externally provided rehabilitation program including clinical exercise prescription.
Demonstrate effective communication in different sports and exercise medicine contexts.

title: Exercise Science Professional Practicum
syllabus_overview: Course Coordinator:Michelle Small (msmall@usc.edu.au)School:School of Health - Sport and Exercise Science
learning_outcomes: Evaluate and apply professional skills to deliver exercise science services in collaboration with clients and other healthcare professionals.
Integrate evidence and theoretical knowledge to assess, prescribe, and deliver exercise interventions for individuals.
Critically reflect on professional practice to enhance self-awareness, social responsibility, and professional development within professional exercise science work settings.

Adhere to ethical, legal, and professional standards of practice according to the Exercise and Sports Science Australia Code of Professional Conduct and Ethical Practice and UniSC Student Placement Code of Conduct.
Practice cultural safety when communicating information, advice, and professional opinions effectively and appropriately to individuals and health professionals.
Design and select appropriate equipment including technology, to implement, monitor, and evaluate client-centred exercise and lifestyle interventions in-person and through tele-practice service.

title: Professional Placement in Sport Studies
syllabus_overview: Course Coordinator:Michelle Small (msmall@usc.edu.au)School:School of Health - Sport and Exercise Science
learning_outcomes: Set work-related learning goals.
Develop enhanced practical skills in targeted areas of sport studies
Develop enhanced practical skills that enable students to work in the community
Learn the value of documenting practical experiences via the use of a portfolio

title: Exercise in Cardiorespiratory and Metabolic Health
syllabus_overview: Course Coordinator:Yuri Kriel (ykriel@usc.edu.au)School:School of Health - Sport and Exercise Science
learning_outcomes: Evaluate the pathophysiological mechanisms associated with cardiorespiratory and metabolic conditions, the comorbid relationship that can exist between pathologies and the influence that exercise has on these issues.
Complete and evaluate results of pre-exercise screening guidelines and identify if medical referral or input is required prior to exercise participation for various clinical populations.
Select, apply and evaluate results of assessment procedures utilised during submaximal and maximal exercise tests for various clinical populations.
Describe and apply the relative and absolute contraindications to exercise and the exercise termination criteria for various clinical populations and justify termination of an exercise test.

Demonstrate the ability to problem solve, formulate and justify appropriate assessments and outcome measures relevant to treatment goals to inform clinical reasoning and to monitor the delivery and outcomes of exercise interventions for various clinical populations.

Critically analyse and disseminate appropriate professional resources and scientific literature through verbal and written platforms to clients, families and relevant health professionals, understanding when further referral is necessary.

title: Exercise in Musculoskeletal Health
syllabus_overview: Course Coordinator:Caitlin Hill (chill3@usc.edu.au)School:School of Health - Sport and Exercise Science
learning_outcomes: Evaluate the role, skills, and scope of practice of an exercise professional in musculoskeletal rehabilitation, multidisciplinary care, referrals and working with other healthcare professionals, within the Australian health system.
Apply and validate knowledge of code of conduct, medical and allied health management of musculoskeletal conditions within the scope of practice of an exercise professional.
Justify clinical decision-making to the recognition of signs and symptoms of musculoskeletal conditions before, during and after exercise and assessment, to inform meaningful intervention.

Identify and act on contraindications and biopsychosocial considerations for musculoskeletal conditions, ensuring inclusive, person-centred, culturally-safe care, modifying services and taking safe and appropriate action (e.g., referral).
Model professional competency to deliver, monitor, document and adapt client assessment, education and exercise-based interventions for clients with musculoskeletal health concerns.
Apply scientific evidence to inform and design service delivery of tailored exercise programs to clients with musculoskeletal conditions.

title: Clinical Skills for Exercise Physiology
syllabus_overview: Course Coordinator:Sonja Coetzee (scoetzee@usc.edu.au)School:School of Health - Sport and Exercise Science
learning_outcomes: Conduct pre-test procedures and sub-maximal clinical exercise test protocols (including ECG & Spirometry), with an understanding of cultural sensitivity and record, interpret and evaluate client data and use laboratory equipment in a clinical setting.

Critically evaluate how commonly prescribed cardiac and pulmonary medications affect physiological responses to exercise, and apply this knowledge to inform safe and effective clinical decision-making.
Assess and interpret cardiac ECG morphologies and lung spirometry tests in a clinical setting.
Integrate clinical reasoning skills and demonstrate competency with cardiac exercise testing with a case study practical examination.

title: Performance Enhancement
syllabus_overview: Course Coordinator:Mark Sayers (msayers@usc.edu.au)School:School of Health - Sport and Exercise Science
learning_outcomes: Apply key theories and principles relating to performance enhancement in an elite sports setting
Create and demonstrate realistic, effective and ethical session plans for different clients from elite sport settings
Critically assess theoretical and empirical research to provide logical and justified practical recommendations
Effectively communicate information to a variety of audiences
Collaborate in multidisciplinary groups to create specific outcomes relating to performance enhancement in elite sport

title: Athlete Coach and Club Welfare
syllabus_overview: Course Coordinator:David Jenkins (djenkins@usc.edu.au)School:School of Health and Behavioural Sciences
learning_outcomes: Critically analyse the impacts of sporting clubs and the effects on individuals, communities and society.
Research and identify issues relating to athlete, coach and officials well-being and recommendations for sporting clubs
Analyse issues affecting club management in communities and make and justify recommendations to address these issues.
Communicate information about sporting club management through written and multi-media modes

title: Exercise Physiology II
syllabus_overview: Course Coordinator:Bridgette O'Malley (bomalley@usc.edu.au)School:School of Health - Sport and Exercise Science
learning_outcomes: Evaluate neuromuscular and cardiovascular function at rest and during exercise, including ensuring the proper calibration and functionality of assessment equipment used during evaluations.
Interpret exercise data and critically evaluate contemporary research in exercise physiology.
Analyse physiological responses and adaptations to exercise based on intensity, duration, frequency, and environmental conditions.
Investigate and analyse physiological responses to different exercise modes and training methodologies.

title: Biomechanics II
syllabus_overview: Course Coordinator:Mark Sayers (msayers@usc.edu.au)School:School of Health - Sport and Exercise Science
learning_outcomes: Utilise biomechanical principles to interpret and analyse kinematic and kinetic data
Investigate the strengths and limitations surrounding data collection using standard biomechanical assessment tools and procedures
Communicate biomechanical findings effectively to both scientific and applied audiences and predict biomechanical assessment outcomes that may affect exercise prescription

Design, conduct and critique a biomechanical assessment on someone with a clinical condition, analyse the data obtained and deliver a series of exercises prescribed by a health professional qualified in clinical exercise prescription
Develop collaborative research skills by working in small teams to evaluate and critique biomechanical data

title: Professional Placement in Sport and Exercise Science
syllabus_overview: Course Coordinator:Michelle Small (msmall@usc.edu.au)School:School of Health - Sport and Exercise Science
learning_outcomes: Set work-related learning goals
Develop enhanced practical skills in targeted areas of sport and exercise science
Develop enhanced practical skills that enable students to work in the community
Learn the value of documenting practical experiences via the use of a portfolio

title: Clinical Exercise Physiology Professional Practicum I
syllabus_overview: Course Coordinator:Ali Valdor (avaldor@usc.edu.au)School:School of Health - Sport and Exercise Science
learning_outcomes: Integrate exercise physiology knowledge and skills to practice effectively in a professional, ethical, inclusive, and collaborative manner across the broad health care system.

Critically evaluate the evidence base and implement relevant knowledge and skills to Accredited Exercise Physiology practice to effectively optimise health status, function, recovery, independence, and participation for all individuals and population groups, whilst practising cultural safety across the full health spectrum.

Safely screen, assess, and evaluate the function, capacity, and health status of individuals and population groups including diverse populations whilst practising cultural safety across various clinical domains.

Interpret data from clinical outcome measures to integrate clinical reasoning to implement safe and effective movement, physical activity, and exercise-based interventions that consider health and treatment needs, and client preferences and goals.

Practise person-centred care to prescribe, deliver, adapt, and evaluate safe and effective evidence-based movement, physical activity, and exercise-based interventions that optimise health status, function, recovery, and independence in collaboration with individuals and population groups, whilst practising cultural safety including diverse populations across the full health spectrum.

Develop reflective practices through self-reflection, seeking and engaging with feedback from supervisors and clients, critically evaluating service delivery and outcomes, and engaging in ongoing learning.

title: Advanced Coaching Science
syllabus_overview: Course Coordinator:Mark Sayers (msayers@usc.edu.au)School:School of Health - Sport and Exercise Science
learning_outcomes: Develop mentoring skills and understand the role of mentoring in personal development
Communicate sport science and coaching principles to both scientific and applied audiences
Interact and work effectively with small groups and colleagues in varied sports contexts
Understanding of the role that exercise plays in individual, community, national and international health

title: Exercise Management in Chronic Disease
syllabus_overview: Course Coordinator:Meegan Walker (mwalker4@usc.edu.au)School:School of Health - Sport and Exercise Science
learning_outcomes: Evaluate the role, skills, and scope of practice of an exercise physiologist in chronic disease management and rehabilitation, multidisciplinary care, discharge, referrals and working with other healthcare professionals within the Australian health system.
Apply and validate knowledge of medical, surgical, and allied health management of chronic diseases within the scope of practice of an exercise physiologist.
Apply and justify clinical decision making to the recognition of signs and symptoms of chronic diseases and complex health conditions in clinical assessment, before, during, and after exercise.

Identify relative and absolute contraindications to exercise for chronic disease rehabilitation and apply this knowledge by taking appropriate action including referral to other health care professionals when required, and modifying exercise assessment and programming when clients are at risk or symptoms are exacerbated.
Critically evaluate and apply scientific evidence to inform and design service delivery of tailored exercise programs to clients with complex presentation and multiple comorbidities.

title: Exercise in Neurological Rehabilitation and Mental Health
syllabus_overview: Course Coordinator:David Borg (dborg@usc.edu.au)School:School of Health - Sport and Exercise Science
learning_outcomes: Evaluate the role, skills and scope of practice of an exercise physiologist in neurological rehabilitation and mental health, multidisciplinary care, discharge, referrals and working with other healthcare professionals within the Australian health system.

Apply and validate knowledge of the pathophysiology, medical, surgical, and allied health management of neurological conditions and mental health care within the scope of practice of an exercise physiologist.
Apply and justify clinical decision making to the recognition of signs and symptoms of neurological and mental health conditions in clinical assessment, before, during, and after exercise.

Identify relative and absolute contraindications to exercise for neurological and mental health conditions and apply this knowledge by taking appropriate action including referral to other health care professionals when required and modifying exercise assessment and programming when clients are at risk or symptoms are exacerbated.
Critically evaluate and apply scientific evidence to inform and design service delivery of tailored exercise programs to clients with neurological and mental health conditions.

title: Exercise in Musculoskeletal Rehabilitation
syllabus_overview: Course Coordinator:Grace Rose (grose1@usc.edu.au)School:School of Health - Sport and Exercise Science
learning_outcomes: Evaluate the role, skills, and scope of practice of an exercise physiologist in musculoskeletal rehabilitation, multidisciplinary care, discharge, referrals and working with other healthcare professionals within the Australian health system.
Apply and validate knowledge of medical, surgical, and allied health management of musculoskeletal conditions within the scope of practice of an exercise physiologist.
Apply and justify clinical decision making to the recognition of signs and symptoms of musculoskeletal conditions and complex presentation in clinical assessment, before, during, and after exercise.

Identify relative and absolute contraindications to exercise for musculoskeletal conditions and apply this knowledge by taking appropriate action including referral to other health care professionals when required and modifying exercise assessment and programming when clients are at risk or symptoms are exacerbated.

Critically evaluate and apply scientific evidence to inform and design service delivery of tailored exercise programs to clients with musculoskeletal conditions and multiple comorbidities in-person and via tele-practice.

assessment_tasks.task_name: Practical Examination and Oral Case Study Defence

title: Case Management and Occupational Rehabilitation
syllabus_overview: Course Coordinator:Meegan Walker (mwalker4@usc.edu.au)School:School of Health - Sport and Exercise Science
learning_outcomes: Evaluate the role, skills and scope of practice of an exercise physiologist in an occupational rehabilitation setting, including referrals and working with other healthcare professionals within the Australian health system.
Explain the legal rights and obligations of working as an exercise physiologist in the Australia health system, including employee compensation systems.

Identify relative and absolute contraindications to exercise for occupational rehabilitation and apply this knowledge by taking appropriate action including delaying physical testing (when required), modifying tests, avoiding tests that present a high risk of aggravation or reinjury and knowing when to refer to another healthcare professional.
Critically evaluate and apply scientific evidence to inform and design service delivery of tailored exercise programs to clients in an occupational rehabilitation setting.

Apply and justify clinical decision making to the recognition of signs and symptoms of clinical conditions (that may affect work capacity) before, during, and after exercise, in order to undertake functional capacity evaluations, clinical assessment, and exercise management suitable for occupational rehabilitation practice.

syllabus_overview: Course Coordinator:Mark Sayers (msayers@usc.edu.au)School:School of Health - Sport and Exercise Science
learning_outcomes: Apply and justify the philosophical, ethical, risk management and technical values and principles of Sport and Exercise science to a research project.
Critique contemporary research in Sport and Exercise Science in your chosen discipline area.
Demonstrate your expertise in selecting and applying research tools, and analysing and interpreting research findings from these instruments.
Justify the relevance of the research design and methodology in relation to the research project

syllabus_overview: Course Coordinator:Mark Sayers (msayers@usc.edu.au)School:School of Health - Sport and Exercise Science
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate your expertise in selecting and applying research tools, and analysing and interpreting research findings from these instruments.
Demonstrate your expertise in applying research tools to meet national standards for the collecting, analysing and interpreting sports science research data.
Collect and Interpret research data and communicate your research findings and their implications for sport science or exercise science to your research colleagues.
Communicate your research findings to other scientists and to non-specialists such as coaches, athletes and the wider community

title: Professional Practice in Health, Sport and Exercise
syllabus_overview: Course Coordinator:Belinda Parmenter (bparmenter@usc.edu.au)School:School of Health - Sport and Exercise Science
learning_outcomes: Describe the structure and function of the Australian healthcare system, understand professional scope of practice and explain the principles of interprofessional collaboration, including appropriate referral pathways within multidisciplinary teams.

Identify and explain the impact of social and cultural determinants of health and stigma on health outcomes and apply basic principles in assessments and interventions for cultural sensitivity and Indigenous health considerations in healthcare interactions using an evidence-based approach.

Articulate the diverse career opportunities within the health professions, particularly in exercise science and exercise physiology, including their professional roles, responsibilities, and pathways for professional self-reflection, -care, -development and national accreditation.

Screen, evaluate and interpret credible sources to identify and inform appropriate health screening and assessment procedures, including screening of relevant social determinants of health, goal setting, and obtaining informed consent in healthcare practice, face to face and via a telehealth service.

Develop an understanding of the importance of protocols for both the client, and healthcare professionals when completing safe, effective and culturally sensitive assessments including risk management and risk assessment concepts associated with the health and assessment of exercise science.

Demonstrate foundational professional conduct and effective communication skills, including verbal, non-verbal, and basic motivational interviewing techniques, while adhering to ethical principles, codes of conduct, and legal responsibilities such as informed consent and accurate record-keeping.

syllabus_overview: Course Coordinator:Theresa Ashford (tashford@usc.edu.au)School:School of Law and Society

Describe and evaluate the concept of ethical responsibility towards present and future generations.
Investigate and evaluate the UN Sustainable Development Goals
Research and communicate information to expert and non expert audiences.

syllabus_overview: Course Coordinator:Harriot Beazley (hbeazley@usc.edu.au)School:School of Law and Society
learning_outcomes: Develop criteria, indicators, measures and targets for assessing sustainability.
To appropriately scope a program evaluation and understand how to undertake it.
Reflect on issues influencing the practice of evaluation.
Effectively undertake and communicate program evaluation.

title: Communicating Sustainability
syllabus_overview: Course Coordinator:Harriot Beazley (hbeazley@usc.edu.au)School:School of Law and Society
learning_outcomes: Communicate sustainability ideas effectively and succinctly by applying communication principles and using credible evidence.
Use written and visual communication strategies for the effective dissemination of sustainability knowledge and ideas.
Analyse and apply a range of communication tools and strategies with reference to purpose, audience, content and the sustainability context.
Use and integrate relevant technologies to enhance the efficacy of sustainability communication strategies.

title: Sustainability Project
syllabus_overview: Course Coordinator:Patrick Nunn (pnunn@usc.edu.au)School:School of Law and Society
learning_outcomes: Research and identify sustainability issues relevant to a particular discipline or professional interest.
Evaluate, analyse and critique how issues may be framed across diverse contexts.
Reflect on and evaluate a range of approaches to address applicable to sustainability issues and consider the implications of them.
Communicate sustainability principles with accuracy and credibility to a target audience.
Develop dynamic approaches for achieving sustainability that anticipate and overcome barriers to the introduction of sustainable practices.

title: Sustainability Problem Solving
syllabus_overview: Course Coordinator:Marcus Bussey (mbussey@usc.edu.au)School:School of Law and Society
learning_outcomes: Identify and describe sustainability issues with reference to sustainability theory and practice.
Recognise complex linkages and feedback mechanisms between social and ecological contexts to identify barriers to and opportunities for sustainable systems.
Reflect on sustainability strategies to propose sustainable solutions to contemporary problems.
Draw on research and sustainability frameworks to imagine and evaluate novel and alternative futures.
Utilise a range of contemporary and practical communication strategies for the effective dissemination of sustainability knowledge and ideas.

title: Social Work Practice in Various Organisational Settings
syllabus_overview: Course Coordinator:Vinathe Sharma-Brymer (vsharmabrymer@usc.edu.au)School:School of Law and Society
learning_outcomes: Review and critique theories, approaches, communication skills, and information relevant to working in human services and indicate how they condition social work practice

Positively and constructively contribute critical perspectives during classroom and assessment activities that display a capacity to sustain focus, engagement, and verbal and nonverbal communication in busy and stimulated environments

Engage in effective professional dialogue with a diverse range of clients, consumers, and other stakeholders, taking into account their varying communication capacities and needs and working effectively with others in a team environment

Apply initiative and judgement in planning, problem-solving, and decision-making, in addition to consulting with other professional practitioners who are contributing to the wellbeing of the people you serve and work with
Act collectively, as well as individually, to bring esteem to the profession through a common purpose of social justice and human rights, inclusion, and wellbeing for people

title: Introduction to Social Work and Human Services
syllabus_overview: Course Coordinator:Krystal McLaughlin (kmclaughlin@usc.edu.au)School:School of Law and Society
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate an ability to respond to evolving practice contexts and situations within the classroom and assessment environments promptly and ethically, showing an understanding of the values, principles, and guidelines described in the Code of Ethics
Apply an intersectional lens to your approach to practice complexities around culture and diversity while working inclusively and respectfully with others

Positively and constructively contribute critical perspectives during classroom and assessment activities that display a capacity to sustain focus, engagement, and verbal and nonverbal communication in busy and stimulated environments
Identify, apply, and promote relevant human rights and social justice concepts, processes, and values in diverse contexts upholding the rights, dignity, and autonomy of all those with whom you work

Engage in effective professional dialogue with a diverse range of clients, consumers, and other stakeholders, taking into account their varying communication capacities and needs and working effectively with others in a team environment
Monitor, evaluate, and review your skills, knowledge, and expertise in a range of oral and written forms across various learning and practice settings

Be an active learner, demonstrating your skills and capacity to work in environments with high workload demands and with competing priorities, requiring your sustained focus, ability to switch between tasks efficiently, and to meet deadlines in managing your professional learning opportunities

title: Introduction to Social Work Practice Theories
syllabus_overview: Course Coordinator:Dimitra Lattas (dlattas@usc.edu.au)School:School of Law and Society
learning_outcomes: Engage with the process of self-reflection and describe how your own environment, beliefs, values and worldviews your role as a social worker.
Apply theoretical concepts to specific practice contexts and are able to adopt or adapt innovations in practice on the basis of a critical assessment of evidence
Apply your knowledge of theory to a particular case study.
Make professional decisions on the basis of a holistic assessment of the needs. strengths, goals and preferences of clients
Demonstrate emerging professional communication skills

title: Mental and Physical Health and Wellbeing
syllabus_overview: Course Coordinator:Tamara Sysak (tsysak@usc.edu.au)School:School of Law and Society
learning_outcomes: Demonstrate knowledge of dominant discourses and constructions of mental and physical health and how they impact the rights, dignity and autonomy of people you work with.
Apply knowledge of the sociocultural factors influencing mental health, physical health and wellbeing, demonstrating the ability to adapt knowledge in diverse contexts.

Demonstrate understanding of the continuing health and social inequalities between Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples and other Australians and how to apply this knowledge when practising in partnership with Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Peoples.
Formulate clear and accurate documentation including notes, assessments and recommendations that are informed by social work theory, practice methods, values and critical reflection.
Articulate use of evidence-based practice to identify and develop interventions based on holistic health and mental health assessments and describe the ethical underpinnings of your approach.
Demonstrate how to assess the nature and level of risk to health and mental health service users and how it to incorporate it in overall assessments.

Assemble relevant information through systematic questioning and discussions with an understanding of how in professional practice you will guided by the lived experience, wishes and preferences of health and mental health service users and their carers/families to the fullest extent possible.

Apply an intersectional lens to recognise the complexity and diversity of personal, social and cultural identity and how this impacts the health and mental health of service users and their access to services.
Actively engage with peers in classroom learning opportunities while being open to new and emerging health and mental health knowledge, research and evidence.
Critically analyse how health and mental health policies effect health outcomes and impact the fair and equitable access to resources.
Articulate the unique scope and contribution social work brings to health/mental health provision in health settings, including when working in interdisciplinary teams.
Participate effectively and respectfully with others in a team environment.
Present a clear, coherent and independent exposition of knowledge and ideas that corresponds with a ‘developing professional’ level.

title: Human Services Placement 1
syllabus_overview: Course Coordinator:Maike Hale (mhale@usc.edu.au)School:School of Law and Society
learning_outcomes: Successfully complete 250 hours of human services practice in accordance with the relevant practice guidelines, in an approved human services setting/organisation.
Undertake professional practice in accordance with accrediting body guidelines and requirements, whilst adhering to appropriate Codes of Ethics.
Demonstrate to a first placement standard, the integration of theory, knowledge, skills and practice guidelines, while practicing in a human services setting.
Develop and begin to demonstrate critical self-reflection in relation to your own practice, values, beliefs and application of ethical responsibilities.
Develop, articulate, assess and evaluate goals for learning and practice in a professional practice setting that incorporate human services theories, skills, knowledge, ethics and values.
Communicate professionally and respectfully with clients, colleagues and community members.
Demonstrate respect and value for others with an understanding of and sensitivity towards issues of cultural diversity, gender and disability.
Demonstrate professional written and verbal communication skills and use appropriate technology for completing reports and other professional written documentation.
Act in a professional manner and in accordance with the relevant Codes of Conduct.
Actively seek feedback on performance and development and apply this to further learning and practice opportunities in a professional setting.
Engage in professional supervision to enhance professional and ethical practice in a human services setting.
Where appropriate, utilise and apply research in practice to address the needs of individuals, groups and communities in society.

title: Health & Mental Health in Australia
syllabus_overview: Course Coordinator:Dyann Ross (dross@usc.edu.au)School:School of Law and Society
learning_outcomes: Describe and explain the historical, conceptual and political foundations to approaches to health and wellbeing.
An ability to use progressive theories to critique modernist models of health interventions in Australia and their impact on service users.
Communicate innovative and creative strategies for social change to address oppression and injustice in the populations health.
Explain the relationship between disadvantaged population groups, dominant discourses and policy agendas and peoples health outcomes.

title: Working with First Nations Peoples and Multicultural Communities
syllabus_overview: Course Coordinator:Vinathe Sharma-Brymer (vsharmabrymer@usc.edu.au)School:School of Law and Society

Apply an intersectional lens to understand and articulate complexities around culture and diversity for engaging respectfully with culturally diverse people

Identify and clearly articulate professional values and ethical practice principles for working alongside Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples and with multicultural communities with cultural responsiveness
Demonstrate and apply critical understanding of theories and research for working alongside Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander and with multicultural communities
Be an active learner demonstrating research, engagement, collaboration, team and group work, and good practice
Demonstrate active contribution of critical perspectives on inter-agency work supporting contemporary developments in Indigenous and Multicultural Social Work area
Work inclusively and respectfully with client to promote their involvement in decision-making

title: Working With Children, Youth and Families

Formulate and document a social work assessment, including analysis of key biopsychosocial risk and protective factors
Keep accurate and comprehensive records and communicate in written and oral modes in a style consistent with an emerging social work professional

Apply a professional knowledge framework informed by critical understanding of contemporary social work theory and research.

Transfer, adapt and apply knowledge in diverse contexts
Demonstrate active learning and openness to new and emerging knowledge, research and evidence informing social work practice
Apply initiative and judgement in planning, problem solving, and decision making

An ability to use progressive theories to critique modernist understandings of, interventions applied and their impact on people living with disability.
An understanding of the integration of critical theory in understanding and responding to current issues in complex and uncertain contexts addressing disablement and ableism
Analyse and assess the relationship between individual and collective responses to disability and their implication for practice and service users
Critically analyse and evaluate disablement approaches within legislative frameworks and policies assessing their impact on individuals with disability
Apply interdisciplinary knowledge, skills and values relating to the study of disability
Work effectively in a team environment
Apply knowledge of legislation, policy and evidence-based practices to formulate service delivery approaches to support people with disability

title: Complexity and Social Work: Group-Based Approaches
syllabus_overview: Course Coordinator:Dyann Ross (dross@usc.edu.au)School:School of Law and Society
learning_outcomes: Identify and describe different types of collective action for social change and their theoretical underpinnings, processes and practices as they relate to diverse population groups and complex human services environments.
Apply knowledge of the historical, environmental, administrative and legislative context to collective action processes utilised in human service settings.
Identify and evaluate foundational processes and considerations for collective action and demonstrate a collective action exercise based on critical practice principles.
Generate principles for future professional practice through critical reflection of use of self in collective action processes.
Apply anti-oppressive and ethical practice frameworks to diverse collective action processes.

title: Social Work Field Education 1
syllabus_overview: Course Coordinator:Dimitra Lattas (dlattas@usc.edu.au)School:School of Law and Society
learning_outcomes: Articulate and apply social work theory, skills and values in a practice situation.
Begin to identify inappropriate or inequitable social policy goals and outcomes, and to consider policy alternatives for achieving equity and effective distribution of social resources.
Begin to analyse organisational systems and processes and societal systems, to identify inequalities
Critically reflect on your own practice and values.
Where appropriate apply research knowledge and skills to undertake ethical research and to disseminate findings
Utilise research in practice to address the needs of individuals, groups and communities, and to further organisational goals and social policy
Engage with individuals, groups and communities in society and apply social work knowledge and skills to enable them to develop their potential and to gain greater control over their lives.
Show respect for and value others with an understanding of and sensitivity towards issues of cultural diversity, gender and disability.
Communicate respectfully with clients, colleagues and community members.
Use written communication and appropriate technology for completing reports and other documentation as required.
Use initiative in learning and practice during the fieldwork placement.
Use all opportunities offered on placement to gain experience working in a human service organisation and develop knowledge of the sector.
Apply the values and ethical principles of social work according to the AASW Code of Ethics (2010).
Act in a professional manner and show self-respect

title: Ethics, Law and the Helping Professions
syllabus_overview: Course Coordinator:Krystal McLaughlin (kmclaughlin@usc.edu.au)School:School of Law and Society

Develop and justify arguments based on understanding of ethical and legal dimensions of practice
Describe and critically evaluate theoretical components of ethical practice
Demonstrate understanding of relevant legislation that influences ethical practice
Demonstrate understanding of need to act in culturally appropriate ways
Develop and demonstrate critical analysis and reflective skills, including ethical use of self in practice
Demonstrate written communication skills relevant to professional ethico-legal issues in the helping professions
Demonstrate active and engaged learning in tutorial settings.
Demonstrate verbal communication skills reflective of an emerging professional helping practitioner.

title: Social Work Field Education 1
syllabus_overview: Course Coordinator:Maike Hale (mhale@usc.edu.au)School:School of Law and Society
learning_outcomes: Articulate and apply social work theory, skills and values in a practice situation and in accordance with the AASW Practice Standards.
Apply and demonstrate the theories, values and ethical principles of social work and in according to the AASW Code of Ethics.
Identify and promote the rights of the people that social workers work with.
Apply an intersectional lens in their approach and practice respectfully and inclusively with regards to culture, gender, disability and diversity more broadly.
Recognise and draw upon the cultural knowledge, experience and wisdom provided by Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Peoples to guide approaches to practice.
Demonstrate respectful, professional communication skills, with clients, colleagues and community members.
Begin to analyse organisational systems and processes and societal systems, to identify inequalities.
Promote fair and equitable access to resources for the people and communities that social workers engage with.
Begin to apply theory, research and social policy to social work practice.
Be an active learner, embracing feedback, new and emerging knowledge, research and evidence informing practice.
Act in a professional manner, working effectively with others in a team environment and in accordance with the relevant Codes of Conduct.
Actively participate in professional social work supervision and learning opportunities to enhance professional and ethical practice.
Critically reflect on their own practice and values.

Demonstrate advanced written communication skills in a TLE-related business context
Analyse sustainable development goals (SDGs) definitions, interpretations and connections and apply to the focal challenges, problems and solutions

Demonstrate effective, professional and persuasive written and oral communication skills.
Understand how to work independently, collaboratively and efficiently in a team environment with internal and external stakeholders.
Demonstrate sound discipline knowledge and skills to explain the nature and scope of the MICE and related Industry.
Evaluate aspects of MICE organisations for their corporate governance and TBL policies and practices.

Articulate effective academic and professional communication for different contexts.

title: Biology
syllabus_overview: Course Coordinator:Luke Ryan (lryan@usc.edu.au)School:School of Education and Tertiary Access
learning_outcomes: Characterise the key features of prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells, the three domains and four kingdoms
Explain how the chemical structure of water results in its four emergent properties
Identify macromolecules, describe their key characteristics and provide examples.
Describe the structure of eukaryotic cells, naming the organelles and recalling their function
Describe cell membrane structure and the types of transport across the cell membrane
Recognise the role of prokaryotes in health, disease and ecosystems
Identify the structures of the human digestive system and describe their function
Outline the fundamental ideas in evolution theory and key themes in biology.
Define basic ecological concepts and outline energy flow and nutrient cycling in ecosystems
Comprehend and effectively communicate scientific biological information.

title: ICT for Academic and Professional Applications
syllabus_overview: Course Coordinator:Sandra Elsom (selsom@usc.edu.au)School:School of Education and Tertiary Access

Demonstrate technical communication skills to transmit information and skills to others.

Reflect upon your learning and draw conclusions about your learning needs, styles and preferences

Research and analyse a chosen organisation and/or industry to develop informed insights and recommendations
Communicate effectively in oral and/or written form, using professional business formats and language

title: Professional People Skills for Study, Community and Society
syllabus_overview: Course Coordinator:Marguerite Westacott (mwestaco@usc.edu.au)School:School of Education and Tertiary Access
learning_outcomes: Use reflective practice principles to identify and analyse intrapersonal, interpersonal, collaboration skills and group processes
Prepare and present a resource or project plan that aims to raise awareness of a current social issue.
Identify social justice principles with reference to a current social issue.
Communicate in a variety of formats to support reasoning, critical reflection and knowledge.
Locate and use key statistics and academic research that apply to a current social issue.

title: International Sport Management Fundamentals
syllabus_overview: Course Coordinator:Kyle Munoz (kmunoz@usc.edu.au)School:School of Business and Creative Industries
learning_outcomes: Describe and compare the structures, governance systems, and organisational models of international sport across different contexts.
Apply sport management and organisational behaviour concepts to analyse issues and practices in global and intercultural sport settings.
Evaluate ethical, inclusive, and sustainable approaches to sport management, including those aligned with the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs).
Analyse emerging global trends and challenges shaping the future of sport management.
Communicate effectively and professionally in international sport business and governance contexts.

assessment_tasks.task_name: Strategy Storyboard – Mapping a Global Sport Issue

title: Managing Tourism, Sports and Events Facilities
syllabus_overview: Course Coordinator:Leonard Vance (lvance@usc.edu.au)School:School of Business and Creative Industries
learning_outcomes: Describe the roles, features, and management considerations of tourism, sport, and event facilities across diverse contexts.
Apply principles of planning, design, and operational logistics to the development and delivery of facilities and events.
Analyse risk, safety, and legal obligations in the management of public-facing facilities.
Evaluate strategies to improve sustainability, accessibility, and community impact in facility operations.
Develop and communicate practical facility management plans using appropriate digital, written, and visual methods.

title: Sport Performance Management
syllabus_overview: Course Coordinator:Kyle Munoz (kmunoz@usc.edu.au)School:School of Business and Creative Industries

Apply knowledge of sport science and interdisciplinary support services to inform practical decisions in high-performance sport management.
Analyse the physical and psychological factors that influence athlete wellbeing, performance, and management.
Evaluate strategies for managing athlete transitions, mental health, and career sustainability.
Communicate sport performance insights and management strategies in appropriate professional formats.

title: Managing Sports Development
syllabus_overview: Course Coordinator:Mohsen Loghmani (mloghmani@usc.edu.au)School:School of Business and Creative Industries

Identify and explain sport development pathways, policies, and practices for developing elite athletes at national and international levels.
Analyse the role of international, national, and community organisations in advancing sport for development and promoting wellbeing and global cooperation.
Evaluate the impact and legacy of sport development initiatives using appropriate evidence and frameworks.
Collaboratively design a strategic program or initiative in sport development that responds to identified needs in elite or community contexts.

assessment_tasks.task_name: Global Sport Development Case Study Showcase

title: Data Analysis in Health
syllabus_overview: Course Coordinator:Georgia Kafer (gkafer@usc.edu.au)School:School of Health - Biomedicine

Use appropriate software tools to support the effective analysis of research data.
Visualise and critically evaluate research outputs to draw meaningful conclusions and identify limitations where relevant.

title: Ethics to Impact
syllabus_overview: Course Coordinator:Georgia Kafer (gkafer@usc.edu.au)School:School of Health - Biomedicine

Communicate and translate research effectively by adapting findings for academic, professional, policy, and community contexts, and evaluating strategies for achieving real-world impact.

Describe the chemical foundations of life.
Apply knowledge of cell structures and functions to solve problems.
Demonstrate foundational skills in scientific communication and critical reasoning.

Analyse physical, social, economic, cultural and psychological factors that shape individuals’ participation and engagement in a broad range of physical activities

Evaluate physical literacy development across the lifespan by critically reflecting on existing physical activity literature, policy and curriculum frameworks and your own movement experiences and teaching philosophy.

title: Research Project Preparation
syllabus_overview: Course Coordinator:Georgia Kafer (gkafer@usc.edu.au)School:School of Health - Biomedicine

Communicate research ideas and proposals clearly and coherently in written and oral forms that demonstrate academic integrity.

Apply knowledge of cells, genes and molecular biology to solve problems.
Conduct experiments to collect, analyse and interpret biological data.
Communicate findings from experiments according to scientific conventions.
Demonstrate competency in skills relevant to the foundational study of cells, genes and molecular biology.

syllabus_overview: Course Coordinator:Georgia Kafer (gkafer@usc.edu.au)School:School of Health - Biomedicine

Critically interpret and synthesise research findings to draw evidence-based conclusions that advance disciplinary understanding or inform professional practice.
Communicate and defend research outcomes effectively through a written thesis and oral presentation that demonstrates critical thinking, academic rigour and responsiveness to feedback.

Reflect on personal health literacy developmental, professional growth and changes in teaching philosophy in relation to contemporary issues that affect youth health.
